headline.en: Color doesn't exist in the world—it's created entirely in your brain

universal_truth.en: We don't see reality as it is; we see our brain's interpretation of it

fun_facts.en: The color you see depends on wavelengths of light—red is about 700nm, violet about 400nm
Mantis shrimp have 16 types of color receptors; humans have only 3
Some languages have no word for blue—and speakers actually perceive it differently

discussion_questions.en: If color is created in the brain, what else might not exist 'out there'?
How might someone with different color perception experience a sunset?
What colors trigger emotions in you—and why might that be?

script.en: Red. Green. Blue. You see these colors so clearly—but here's the thing: there is no color in the physical world. Only wavelengths of electromagnetic radiation. Color exists nowhere but inside your brain. Today, we explore this beautiful illusion.

text.en: I want to learn something new

response.en: Perfect. Curiosity is the first step to understanding. Let's explore this together.
That curiosity is exactly what we need. Let's dive in and discover something amazing.

script.en: If color is a brain construction, why do we all mostly agree on what's red and what's blue? Is color real? Imaginary? And could two people see the same sky completely differently?

prompt.en: Do we all see colors the same way?

text.en: Probably not—color perception varies between individuals

response.en: Correct. Color is subjective. We can never be certain others see what we see.

text.en: Yes—the wavelengths are objective so color must be too

response.en: Wavelengths are objective, but the experience of color is...

script.en: Light is electromagnetic radiation. What we call red is wavelengths around 700 nanometers; violet is around 400. Your eyes have three types of cone cells—sensitive to short, medium, and long wavelengths. Your brain combines their signals into the rich experience of color.

prompt.en: What's your first impression of "Wavelengths and Cones"?

text.en: This confirms what I already knew

response.en: Great foundation! Now let's build on that knowledge with something you might not expect...
Perfect starting point! This insight will connect to even more surprising facts ahead.

script.en: Humans have 3 color receptors. Mantis shrimp have 16. What do they see that we can't? Colors we don't have names for—colors we literally can't imagine. There are more colors in the universe than any creature can perceive.

prompt.en: How does this connect to what you already know?

response.en: Exactly. These connections are how knowledge becomes understanding.

text.en: I need to think about this more

response.en: That's a good instinct. Deep understanding takes time. The next fact will help clarify.

script.en: Some languages don't distinguish blue from green—they use one word for both. Studies show speakers of these languages are slower to distinguish blue and green objects. The words we have actually shape what we see. Language programs perception.

prompt.en: What surprises you most about this?

text.en: I never thought about it this way

response.en: That shift in perspective is exactly the point. New angles reveal new truths.
That's learning in action. When understanding shifts, you're really getting it.

script.en: Here's today's wisdom: Color reminds us that we don't see the world—we see our brain's interpretation of it. Reality is always filtered through the lens of the perceiver. Humility about perception is wisdom about truth.

prompt.en: What resonates most with you today?

response.en: That central truth will stay with you. Let it guide your thinking.
Application is where knowledge becomes wisdom. That's the real learning.

script.en: That's Day 22. Tomorrow, we'll discover patterns hidden everywhere. Until then, look around—and remember: all that color exists only in your mind.

prompt.en: Before you go—what will you take from today?

response.en: Reflection deepens learning. Let these ideas simmer in your mind.
Teaching others is the best way to learn. You've already begun the ripple.

learning_objective.en: Heighten awareness of color in your environment

activity.en: Look around your current environment and count how many distinct colors you can identify. Push past the obvious—notice subtle variations and shades. Try to find at least 20 different colors. Appreciate that all of them exist only in your mind.
